planting.note: Set container plants in part shade to shade in spring or fall, digging a hole twice the pot width and backfilling with the crown slightly above grade; keep evenly moist while roots establish.

directions: Big Daddy is a mophead hydrangea grown for exceptionally oversized flower heads that shift from pink to blue depending on soil acidity. Give it part shade to shade and consistently moist, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool through summer. It needs little pruning and responds well to an annual spring feeding, rewarding growers with huge rounded blooms through the summer season.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection official site

planting.note: Plant container stock in full sun to part shade in spring or fall, positioning the crown 1-2 inches above grade and mulching lightly; established plants tolerate a wide range of soils.

directions: Moon Dance is a panicle hydrangea producing dense, conical clusters of creamy white blooms on sturdy stems strong enough to hold the flowers upright without staking. It tolerates more sun than mophead types and adapts to average garden soil once established. Deadheading spent panicles encourages continued flowering through summer, and little to no structural pruning is needed to maintain its upright form.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection official site

planting.note: Set plants in full sun in spring, digging a hole twice the container width and settling the crown slightly above grade; mulch and water deeply to establish.

directions: Sweet Starlight is a compact panicle hydrangea bred to stay under four feet while still producing abundant blooms in full sun. Flowers open bright white and gradually age to an antique pink, giving the shrub two-toned color through the season on strong, self-supporting stems. Deadheading encourages repeat flowering, and the plant otherwise needs minimal pruning to keep a tidy, rounded shape.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection official site

planting.note: Plant container stock in part sun to shade in spring or fall, backfilling so the crown sits 1-2 inches above grade, then mulch and water in well.

directions: Snowcicle is a native oakleaf hydrangea selected for unusually long, 12 to 14 inch double flower spikes held on sturdy stems. Blooms open creamy white and deepen to rose-red as they age, adding to the oakleaf's already strong multi-season appeal of exfoliating bark and purple-to-orange fall foliage. It tolerates drier conditions once established better than many hydrangeas and needs little more than light shaping after its spring bloom.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection official site

planting.note: Plant in partial shade to shade in spring or fall, setting the crown 1-2 inches above grade and mulching; keep soil consistently moist while new roots form.

directions: Blast from the Pastel is a mophead hydrangea whose florets open white and are flecked with soft yellow, blue, and pink accents, giving each flower head a mottled, confetti-like look rather than a single uniform color. It reblooms through the season, so promptly removing spent flower heads encourages fresh color to keep coming. Suited to borders, mass plantings, and cut-flower use, it performs best with consistent moisture and protection from the hottest afternoon sun.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection official site

planting.note: Set container plants in part shade to shade in spring, positioning the crown 1-2 inches above grade and mulching well; this compact selection suits foundation plantings and containers.

directions: Heart Throb is a compact mophead hydrangea that blooms on both old and new wood, extending its color display across three seasons. Flowers open a deep red edged in green and gradually shift toward green tones brushed with red as they mature, giving the shrub an unusually long-lasting, evolving bloom display. It stays small enough for foundation plantings or large containers and needs essentially no pruning to maintain its rounded form.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection official site

planting.note: Plant in full sun in spring or fall, backfilling with the crown 1-2 inches above grade and mulching; this upright panicle type tolerates average garden soil once established.

directions: White Wedding is a panicle hydrangea with sturdy, upright stems that hold large, dense, pillow-shaped white flower clusters without flopping over. The oversized blooms make it a favorite for cutting as well as garden display, and its tolerance for full sun sets it apart from many shade-loving mophead types. Little pruning is required, and deadheading spent clusters can prompt additional blooms through the season.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection official site

planting.note: Plant container stock in full sun to part shade in fall or spring, setting the crown 1-2 inches above grade and mulching; an upright, dense habit makes it well suited to screening.

directions: Fall Fantasy is a sasanqua camellia bred for an especially heavy fall bloom, producing rose-form pink flowers that can appear in clusters of up to a dozen per branch tip. Its upright, dense growth habit makes it a strong candidate for hedges and privacy screens as well as a specimen planting. Grow it in acidic, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade in hotter climates, and prune lightly after flowering if shaping is desired.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection official site

planting.note: Plant in full sun to part shade in fall or spring, excavating a hole twice the root ball width and setting the crown 1-2 inches above grade; mulch to conserve moisture.

directions: Diana is a larger-growing sasanqua camellia that produces white, semi-double to informal double flowers with bright yellow centers from October into November. Its ultimate size, reaching eight to ten feet tall, makes it a good choice for a background screen, hedge, or small specimen tree rather than a compact foundation planting. Site it in acidic, well-drained soil with morning sun and some afternoon protection in the hottest climates, and prune after bloom in spring if a more restrained shape is wanted.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection official site
